If you want to move 'right' in space, you eject something to your 'left' and thanks to Newton's third law, for every action there's an equal but opposite action, you end up moving to the 'right.' This has a major consequence for space travel. It means you need a ton of 'stuff' to eject. The further you want to go the more you need. But the more 'stuff' you bring, the more that you need to eject in order to get to the same speed. 'The tyranny of the rocket equation.'

The EM drive changes all of this. If you can create even a whisper of thrust without expelling anything then suddenly you change the problem from one of mass to one of energy generation which is far easier to resolve. You could "refuel" ships with, for instance, solar energy. Remember in space there is no air resistance. So you don't slow down. Accelerate something a fraction of a meter per second and you'll be at relativistic (near the speed of light) velocities eventually. And of course it's also likely that the effective thrust will be able to be scaled up.

This is all also the reason that there's so much scientific 'consternation' about the validity of the EM drive. One of the fundamental observations we've seen in everything in our universe is the conservation of momentum. The effective momentum in a system never changes. Momentum in one direction is cancelled out by momentum in another. The EM drive seems to violate this observation. So it's either acting in a way that's unlike anything ever observed in the universe, or it's not actually doing what it seems to be doing.
